text:
Yes—it's coherent to say a person can be harmed by something that happens after their death, though the harm is of a distinctive kind.

### Position
A plausible view is this: a person can be harmed whenever their interests are set back, even if they never experience that setback. On this account, harm does not require felt suffering. While alive, people often have interests that extend beyond their lifespan: that their children flourish, that their work be preserved, that promises made to them be kept, that their name not be slandered. If those interests are defeated after death, then something bad has happened *for them*, not just for the living.

The clearest case is the broken promise. Suppose I promise a dying friend to publish her manuscript, then destroy it after she dies. She never learns this, and she feels no pain. Still, it seems more than merely regrettable for us; it seems a wrong *to her*. The natural explanation is that her interest in the manuscript’s survival has been frustrated, and so she has been harmed posthumously.

### Why this is coherent
The main objection is that harm requires a subject who exists at the time of the harm. If the person no longer exists, who is there to be harmed? But many harms already do not depend on awareness. A person can be betrayed behind their back, deceived without ever finding out, or mocked in secret. We still call these harms because they damage the person's welfare or interests, not because they produce a certain sensation.

Posthumous harm extends the same idea one step further. The event occurs later, but it defeats an interest the person had while alive. The timing is unusual, but not unintelligible.

### A limitation
Still, we should distinguish posthumous harm from ordinary experiential harm. The dead do not suffer, and no new unpleasant experience is added to their lives. So the harm is not a matter of pain but of their life going worse in a broader sense: their projects, commitments, and standing are retrospectively undermined.

### Implications for wills
If this is right, wills matter morally, not just legally. Ignoring a person’s valid will is not only an injury to heirs or a violation of social rules; it can also be a wrong to the deceased, because it defeats their surviving intentions about their property, body, or legacy. This supports taking testamentary wishes seriously, though not absolutely. The living may still have stronger claims—say, if a will requires injustice or serious waste—but there is at least a genuine reason in favor of honoring it.

### Implications for posthumous reputation
The same applies to reputation. Defaming the dead can wrong them, because many people have a strong interest in how they are remembered. Destroying a reputation through lies can therefore count as a posthumous harm. By contrast, truthful criticism is different. If new evidence reveals that a celebrated figure acted badly, reporting it may damage their reputation, but not necessarily wrong them; a person has no legitimate interest in being falsely praised. So the view supports protection against slander of the dead more readily than protection against truthful historical reassessment.

### Conclusion
So, yes: it is coherent to say the dead can be harmed by later events, provided harm is understood as the frustration of a person’s interests rather than as felt suffering. That implies we have real moral reasons to respect wills and to avoid false attacks on the dead’s reputation, even though those reasons can sometimes be outweighed by the needs and rights of the living.
